Question 1 of 11 · Is there a Creator?

Can we know that anything is real?

Short answer

Yes. Even doubting proves that something is real, and no one lives as if nothing is.

Objections

What people say against this, and our answer. Open one to read it.

You might say“Reality itself might not exist”

Our answer

Even your doubt is proof that something is real.

The one thing you cannot doubt

René Descartes tried to doubt everything he could: his senses, the physical world, even simple sums like two plus three. One thing survived the doubt. While he was thinking, he had to exist. It is usually summed up as “I think, therefore I am.”

This doesn't mean we have perfect knowledge of reality. It means that something exists — including you, your experience, and the act of questioning. That's enough to build on.

ArticleStanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Descartes’ Epistemology↗(opens in a new tab)
You might say“I just can't be certain about anything”

Our answer

Total skepticism is a position no one actually lives by.

The gap between theory and practice

The ancient skeptics faced a famous objection, known as the apraxia charge: without beliefs, how can anyone act? If you truly can’t know whether fire burns, why not touch it?

The philosopher David Hume admitted that his own doubts did not survive ordinary life:

I dine, I play a game of back-gammon, I converse, and am merry with my friends; and when after three or four hour's amusement, I wou'd return to these speculations, they appear so cold, and strain'd, and ridiculous, that I cannot find in my heart to enter into them any farther.

David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature (1739), 1.4.7

You avoid cars, trust floors to hold you, expect the sun to rise. These aren't leaps of faith — they're rational inferences from consistent experience. The consistency of reality is itself evidence worth examining. A reality that behaves according to stable, mathematical laws points to something deeper than randomness.

ArticleStanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Ancient Skepticism↗(opens in a new tab)BookDavid Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, 1.4.7↗(opens in a new tab)
You might say“Maybe we're living in a simulation”

Our answer

If we're in a simulation, that confirms a Creator — it doesn't remove one.

Simulation theory and the question of origins

In 2003 the philosopher Nick Bostrom argued that at least one of three things is true, and one of them is that “we are almost certainly living in a computer simulation.” But notice what that would mean: the simulation had to be designed by someone. That designer is real, exists outside our reality, and brought our reality into being. The simulation idea doesn’t remove a Creator. It describes one.

The simulation hypothesis also pushes the question back rather than answering it. Who created the civilisation that runs the simulation? What are the physical laws of their reality? You still need a first cause — an uncaused originator — at some level. Moving the origin of our universe one level up doesn't escape the need for an ultimate beginning.

StudyNick Bostrom, Philosophical Quarterly (2003)↗(opens in a new tab)
